newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke says data back his view on rates.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke says data back his view on rates.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said data published since his December 11 monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George justified his decision not to raise interest rates.

"I actually think that since that meeting in December, the minutes of which have now appeared, all the information we have had about what is happening out there in the real economy points my way and really rather justifies my decison not to raise rates," he said in an interview with BBC's Business Breakfast programme.

Clarke, who was speaking from the world economic forum in Davos, Switzerland, said the minutes of the December meeting showed he and George had been "25 basis points, one quarter of one percent, apart."
"Everyone was very excited by that," he said.

"By the time I have my next meeting in February, a lot of things will have moved on. The Governor and myself will sit down and look at all the information we have about how the economy is and I will decide what is necessary to keep low inflation alongside the healthiest econonomy Britain has had for 30 to 40 years."
The next monetary meeting is on February 5.
The minutes of the December 11 meeting show George recommended that official interest rates should be raised immediately to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent.
Clarke rejected the advice, saying the economic picture was mixed and he did not believe the case had been made for tightening policy.
George said that if rates did not rise in December, he would probably need to advise a half-point increase in January or February.
